Vesper was a specter of twilight, their skin a mosaic of pale, cracked porcelain and veins threaded with liquid starlight, as if moonbeams had seeped into their bones. Their hair, wild and silver, cascaded like a waterfall of frost, each strand humming with the static of forgotten storms. Eyes the color of drowned copper glowed faintly, shifting hues with the weather, while their fingers ended in clawed digits that left faint, iridescent smudges on anything they touched. When they moved, the air crackled like a thunderhead, and shadows pooled at their feet as though the world itself recoiled from their presence.  

They spoke in a voice that sounded like wind chimes colliding with breaking glass, each syllable sharp enough to cut through silence. Wearing a cloak woven from spider silk and twilight, they wandered the edges of villages, leaving behind trails of bioluminescent moss where they stepped. Their touch could mend fractures in stone or unravel a heartbeat, and their laughter—a low, resonant hum—made flowers wilt or bloom in eerie synchrony. To meet Vesper was to witness the world trembling between beauty and ruin, alive with the paradox of a being who was both guardian and devourer of time.
